title: Not two
hook: the poem ends: faith and mind are not two

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that turns the search around: don't seek the true. Your line: just stop holding opinions. Which topic did you leave without a verdict? Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

Some poems save their biggest image for the last line: a sunset, a storm, a door closing. The Xinxin Ming does something stranger. It ends by taking its own title, faith and mind, and folding the two words together until there is no gap between them. After all the warnings about picking and choosing, about the hair's breadth and the opinions, the last word it leaves is a pair of plain words. Not two. Today we read the ending of the poem.
screen: `SOME POEMS END ON AN IMAGE.` → `THIS ONE FOLDS ITS TITLE.` → `TWO PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the last lines. In paraphrase, the poem closes: faith and mind are not two; not two is faith in mind. Then it says the way is beyond words, not a matter of past, future or present. Second, notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say faith and mind are one. Why not? Because one is just another thing to hold. Earlier in the poem there is a line for exactly this: two exists because of one, so don't cling even to the one. Chinese Buddhist texts use this word, not two, for what English often calls nonduality, and its whole job is to stop the mind landing anywhere: not split into two, and not stuck on one either. Third, it is practical. In paraphrase, the poem advises: if you want to come into accord with the way quickly, just say: not two. Some translators add, when doubt arises. It is less a doctrine to agree with than a tool to use, right when the mind starts dividing the moment into what I want and what I don't. Fourth, the title, folded shut. This week the poem began with picking and choosing, the mind splitting its day into liked and disliked. It ends with the trust and the mind that trusts refusing to come apart. There's no faith standing over here, aimed at a mind over there. In the poem's last breath, the trusting and the trusted are not two. And that brings us back to where the week started: the great way is not hard.
screen: `THE LAST LINES: NOT TWO.` · `NOT TWO IS NOT 'ONE'.` · `TO ACCORD QUICKLY, SAY IT.` · `THE TITLE, FOLDED SHUT.` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath settle. Let the hands rest in the oval from earlier in the week, thumb tips just touching. Feel the point where they meet. Which thumb is touching, and which is being touched? Gently look for the line where one stops and the other starts. Don't force it, and don't decide anything about it. If a thought comes, like 'is this right?', you can answer it the way the poem does, quietly: not two. Then come back to the thumbs. The bell holds the time.
Not two. The last word of the Xinxin Ming: faith and mind are not two, and the poem won't let you settle on one either. Today's word.
Your line: not two. Today, when the moment splits into what you want and what you've got, say it once, quietly. Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Zen and Chan students who chant the Xinxin Ming end on these lines, and some teachers offer 'not two' as a phrase to return to in sitting when the mind starts to divide.

original.note: Chinese (bu er): 'not two', the poem's last word and a term Chinese Buddhist texts use for nonduality.

trapdoor: what you thought: not two means everything melts into one.
what it means: faith and mind, the trusting and the trusted, don't come apart, and the mind isn't asked to hold 'one' instead.
what a scholar hears: the closing lines fold the title into 不二, 'not two': faith-mind not two, not-two faith-mind.

sources.work: Xinxin Ming (Faith in Mind), attributed to Sengcan
